topic: Bayes' Theorem and Independence: The Logic of Updating Beliefs
target_audience: Introductory University Students or Advanced High School Students

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem and Independence: The Logic of Updating Beliefs
outline.target_audience: Introductory University Students or Advanced High School Students

sections.title: The Foundation: Understanding Independence
sections.content: Introduce the concept of Independence. Two events are independent if the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other. Visually, represent this as two separate Venn diagram circles where the intersection area is exactly P(A) * P(B).
sections.example: Imagine flipping a coin and rolling a die. The coin landing on 'Heads' (Event A) has no influence on the die landing on '6' (Event B). P(A and B) is simply 1/2 * 1/6 = 1/12.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & Sample Space Shrinking
sections.content: Explain that when events are NOT independent, we use Conditional Probability P(A|B). Graphically, show the 'Universe' (Sample Space) shrinking from the whole rectangle to only the area of circle B. We are now looking for the fraction of B that is also A.
sections.example: In a forest of 100 animals, 20 are rare blue birds. If it is raining, blue birds are harder to find. Knowing 'It is Raining' (Event B) changes the probability of 'Seeing a Blue Bird' (Event A).

sections.title: The Bridge: Bayes' Theorem Formula
sections.content: Derive Bayes' Theorem visually: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Use an 'Area Model' or 'Tree Diagram' animation to show how we move from a Prior probability P(A) to a Posterior probability P(A|B) based on new evidence B.
sections.example: Think of P(A) as your 'Initial Guess' and P(B|A)/P(B) as the 'Strength of Evidence' that updates your guess.

sections.title: Application: The Robot Spy Detector Paradox
sections.content: Apply the theorem to a classic 'False Positive' scenario. Even with a highly accurate detector, if a condition is rare (Independence of the test vs. the base rate), the result can be surprising. Use a 2x2 grid animation to show population counts.
sections.example: A village has 1% Secret Agents. A Security Robot has a 95% accuracy rate (P(Ping|Agent)=0.95). If the Robot pings a villager, most people assume there is a 95% chance they are an agent. Using Bayes, we show the actual probability is much lower (~16%) because agents are so rare.

sections.title: Summary: Independence vs. Bayesian Updating
sections.content: Consolidate the learning. Independence means no update is needed. Bayes' Theorem is the mathematical tool for when events are dependent and we must update our knowledge based on evidence. End with a visual recap of the 'Shrinking Sample Space'.
sections.example: Recap: Independence is like two parallel tracks; Bayes' Theorem is like a magnifying glass focusing on a specific part of the map based on what we see.

storyboard.title: The Foundation: Understanding Independence
lecture_lines: Events are independent if they don't affect each other.
A coin flip doesn't change a die roll result.
One outcome gives no information about the other.
Their joint probability is the product of individual probabilities.
Visually, the intersection area matches this product.
animations: Display a coin (Circle labeled A, #ADD8E6) and a die (Square labeled B, #FFB6C1) on opposite sides of the screen.
Flash the coin (A) and then the die (B), showing no interaction or movement between them.
Move A and B to center, show formula "P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)" in #FFFFFF below them.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & Sample Space Shrinking
lecture_lines: Dependency requires using conditional probability instead.
Probability of A given B focuses on circle B.
The sample space shrinks from everything to only B.
We calculate the fraction of B that is A.
This shift represents our updated knowledge.
animations: Show a large white rectangle (Universe). Place a blue circle (A, #0000FF) and a green circle (B, #00FF00) overlapping.
Fade out everything outside circle B. Scale circle B to fill the center of the screen.
Highlight the intersection (A \cap B) in #FFFF00 and label it "P(A|B)".

storyboard.title: The Bridge: Bayes' Theorem Formula
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem updates a prior belief with new evidence.
It scales our initial guess by evidence strength.
The formula yields an updated posterior probability.
animations: Show "P(A)" labeled "Prior" in #ADD8E6 on the left.
An arrow labeled "Evidence P(B|A) / P(B)" (#FFFFFF) moves from "Prior" to a new term "P(A|B)".
Display the full formula "P(A|B) = [P(B|A) \times P(A)] / P(B)" in center, #FFFF00.

storyboard.title: Application: The Robot Spy Detector Paradox
lecture_lines: Rare events make false positives very likely.
Suppose only one percent of people are secret agents.
A robot detector is ninety-five percent accurate.
A positive ping still leaves the probability low.
Most pings come from the large non-agent population.
animations: Display a 10x10 grid of small grey squares. Color one square red (#FF0000) to represent the 1% agent.
Highlight the 1 red square and 5 grey squares (false positives) with a pulsing yellow border (#FFFF00).
Fade out all squares except the 6 highlighted ones. Show the ratio 1/6 (~16.7%) prominently.

storyboard.title: Summary: Independence vs. Bayesian Updating
lecture_lines: Independence requires no updates to our knowledge.
Bayes' Theorem provides the math for learning from data.
Evidence always shrinks the space of possibilities.
animations: Show two parallel blue lines (#0000FF) moving across the screen without touching.
Show a magnifying glass (#FFFFFF) zooming in on an intersection of two overlapping circles.
Display "Independence" vs "Bayesian Update" on screen. Flash the text "Update Your World" in #FFFF00.
